2017B16.goal: We count positive integers up to $2017$ whose decimal form contains at least one $0$. Counting "has a zero" directly is messy; counting "no zeros" by number of digits is easy.

tools.name: Complementary counting
tools.why: "No zeros" means every digit is $1$–$9$, a simple product.

tools.name: Counting digit strings
tools.why: Each of the $k$ digits has $9$ choices.

2017B16.approach: Split by number of digits. For each length, subtract the zero-free numbers from the total. The range $2000$–$2017$ is a small special case: every one of them contains a $0$.

steps.title: Up to three digits
steps.explain: One digit: none. Two digits: $90-81=9$ ($10,20,\ldots,90$). Three digits: $900-729=171$.

check.q: How many $3$-digit numbers have no zero?

steps.title: Four digits
steps.explain: $1000$–$1999$: $1000$ numbers, of which $9^3=729$ have no zero (the first digit is $1$). So $271$. $2000$–$2017$: all $18$ contain a $0$.

check.q: How many numbers from $1000$ to $1999$ contain a $0$?

2017B16.bridge: Count by number of digits, subtracting the zero-free numbers.
2017B16.shortcut: Count zero-free numbers up to $1999$: $9+81+729+729=1548$, so $1999-1548=451$ have a zero; add $18$.
traps: Using $9^4$ for $1000$–$1999$ (the first digit is fixed as $1$).
2017B16.recognize: "How many contain digit $d$": count the complement (no $d$) digit by digit.

2017B17.goal: A monotonous number has strictly increasing or strictly decreasing digits (one-digit numbers count). Such a number is determined by its set of digits, so we count digit sets.

tools.name: Set to number
tools.fact: \text{A set of digits gives exactly one increasing and one decreasing arrangement}
tools.why: Strict order is forced by the set.

tools.name: Counting subsets
tools.why: Each element is in or out.

tools.name: Inclusion–exclusion
tools.why: One-digit numbers are both increasing and decreasing.

2017B17.approach: Increasing numbers cannot contain $0$ (it would have to be the leading digit): subsets of $\{1,\ldots,9\}$. Decreasing numbers may end in $0$: subsets of $\{0,\ldots,9\}$ except $\{0\}$. Subtract the one-digit numbers counted twice.

steps.title: Increasing
steps.explain: Any nonempty subset of $\{1,\ldots,9\}$ in increasing order: $2^9-1=511$.

check.q: Why can't an increasing number contain $0$?

steps.title: Decreasing
steps.explain: Any nonempty subset of $\{0,\ldots,9\}$ in decreasing order, except $\{0\}$ (not positive): $2^{10}-2=1022$.

steps.title: Remove double counts
steps.explain: One-digit numbers $1$–$9$ were counted in both: $511+1022-9=1524$.

2017B17.bridge: Count digit subsets for increasing and decreasing numbers and subtract the overlap.
solution: Decreasing: nonempty subsets of $\{0..9\}$ other than $\{0\}$: $1022$.
One-digit numbers are in both: subtract $9$.
2017B17.shortcut: Strictly monotone numbers correspond to subsets; just handle $0$ and the one-digit overlap.
traps: Forgetting to subtract the one-digit overlap.
2017B17.recognize: Numbers with strictly increasing/decreasing digits are subsets of digits; count subsets.

2017B18.goal: Six disks arranged in a triangle (rows of $1,2,3$) are painted $3$ blue, $2$ red, $1$ green. Paintings related by a rotation or reflection of the triangle count as the same. We count distinct paintings using Burnside's lemma.

tools.name: Burnside's lemma
tools.why: Average the number of colourings each symmetry leaves unchanged.

tools.name: Multinomial count
tools.why: Colourings before identifying symmetric ones.

tools.name: Symmetries of the triangle
tools.why: The figure has the symmetry of an equilateral triangle.

2017B18.approach: Use Burnside: the identity fixes all $60$ colourings; rotations cycle the three corner disks and the three side disks, so a fixed colouring would need colour counts in multiples of $3$ (impossible). Each reflection fixes two disks and swaps two pairs; count colourings consistent with that.

steps.title: Identity and rotations
steps.explain: Identity: $60$. A $120^\circ$ rotation moves corners in a $3$-cycle and side disks in a $3$-cycle, so each cycle must be one colour. Counts $3,2,1$ cannot be made from two blocks of $3$: $0$ fixed.

check.q: Can colour counts $3,2,1$ be made from two groups of $3$ same-coloured disks?
check.why: Each colour count would be $0,3$ or $6$.

steps.title: Reflections
steps.explain: A reflection fixes a corner disk and the middle disk of the opposite side, and swaps two pairs. Green (count $1$) must be on a fixed disk ($2$ choices). The other fixed disk must be blue, and the pairs are one blue pair and one red pair ($2$ ways). So $4$ per reflection, $12$ in total.

check.q: How many fixed colourings for one reflection?

2017B18.bridge: Apply Burnside: count colourings fixed by each of the $6$ symmetries.
solution: The two rotations fix none (counts are not multiples of $3$).
Each of the three reflections fixes $4$ (green on a fixed disk, then the pairs).
2017B18.shortcut: Without Burnside: $60$ colourings in orbits of size $6$ or $3$; the $12$ symmetric ones form orbits of size $3$: $\tfrac{60-12}{6}+\tfrac{12}{3}=8+4$.
traps: Forgetting the reflections fix two disks each.
2017B18.recognize: Counting colourings up to rotation and reflection: Burnside's lemma (average fixed colourings).

2017B19.goal: Each side of equilateral triangle $ABC$ is extended beyond a vertex by $3$ times its length. We want $[A'B'C']:[ABC]$. The big triangle is $ABC$ plus three congruent outer triangles.

tools.name: Area with an included angle
tools.why: Base times height, with height $b\sin C$.

tools.name: Supplementary angle
tools.why: $\sin(180^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta$.

2017B19.approach: Triangle $A'B'C'$ splits into $ABC$ and three triangles like $AA'B'$. In $AA'B'$, the sides at $A$ are $AA'=3$ and $AB'=4$ (taking $AB=1$), with angle $120^\circ$. Compare its area with $ABC$ using $\tfrac12ab\sin C$.

steps.title: One outer triangle
steps.explain: Take side $1$. In $\triangle A'AB'$: $AA'=3$, $AB'=AB+BB'=4$, and the angle at $A$ is $180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$. Area $\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot4\sin120^\circ$.

steps.title: Compare with $ABC$
steps.explain: $[ABC]=\tfrac12\cdot1\cdot1\sin60^\circ$. Since $\sin120^\circ=\sin60^\circ$, each outer triangle is $12$ times $[ABC]$.

steps.title: Total
steps.explain: $[A'B'C']=[ABC]+3\cdot12[ABC]=37[ABC]$.

2017B19.bridge: Split $A'B'C'$ into $ABC$ and three outer triangles; compare areas with $\tfrac12ab\sin C$.
solution: With side $1$: $\triangle A'AB'$ has sides $3$ and $4$ around a $120^\circ$ angle.
There are three such triangles plus $ABC$.
2017B19.shortcut: General rule: extending each side by $k$ times gives ratio $1+3k(k+1)$; here $1+3\cdot3\cdot4=37$.
traps: Assuming $A'B'C'$ is $4$ times larger in side (it is rotated, not similar by $4$).
2017B19.recognize: Extended-side triangles: decompose into the original plus outer triangles and use $\tfrac12ab\sin C$ with supplementary angles.

2017B20.goal: A random divisor of $21!$ is chosen. We want the probability it is odd. Write $21!=2^e\cdot m$ with $m$ odd; odd divisors are the divisors of $m$.

tools.name: Legendre's formula
tools.why: Count multiples of $2,4,8,16$.

tools.name: Divisor counting
tools.why: Choose the power of $2$ independently of the odd part.

2017B20.approach: Total divisors are $(e+1)\cdot d(m)$; odd divisors are $d(m)$. The probability is $\tfrac1{e+1}$, so only the exponent of $2$ matters.

steps.title: Probability
steps.explain: Divisors $2^j\cdot d$ with $0\le j\le18$ and $d\mid m$; odd ones have $j=0$. Probability $\tfrac{1}{19}$.

check.q: If $n=2^4\cdot m$ with $m$ odd, what fraction of divisors are odd?

solution: Divisors are $2^jd$, $0\le j\le18$, $d\mid m$; exactly those with $j=0$ are odd.
2017B20.shortcut: Only the power of $2$ matters; the huge divisor count is irrelevant.
2017B20.recognize: Probability a random divisor has some prime-power property: separate that prime's exponent; it is independent of the rest.

2017B21.goal: In the $6$-$8$-$10$ right triangle, $D$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse $BC$. We want the sum of the inradii of triangles $ADB$ and $ADC$. Each inradius is area over semiperimeter.

tools.name: Median to the hypotenuse
tools.why: The midpoint of the hypotenuse is the circumcentre, equidistant from all three vertices.

tools.name: Median splits area in half
tools.why: Same height from $A$, equal bases $BD=DC$.

tools.name: Inradius
tools.why: Area $=rs$.

2017B21.approach: Find all side lengths: $AD=5$, $BD=DC=5$. Each half has area $12$. Compute both semiperimeters and inradii.

steps.title: Side lengths
steps.explain: $BC=10$ is the hypotenuse (right angle at $A$). $D$ is the midpoint, so $BD=DC=5$ and $AD=5$. Triangles: $ADB$ with sides $5,5,6$; $ADC$ with sides $5,5,8$.

check.q: In a right triangle with hypotenuse $14$, how long is the median to the hypotenuse?

steps.title: Inradii
steps.explain: Both areas are $12$. $ADB$: $s=8$, $r=\tfrac{12}8=\tfrac32$. $ADC$: $s=9$, $r=\tfrac{12}9=\tfrac43$.

check.q: A triangle with area $12$ and semiperimeter $9$ has inradius?

steps.title: Sum
steps.explain: $\tfrac32+\tfrac43=\tfrac{17}6$.

2017B21.bridge: Use $AD=5$, equal half-areas $12$, and $r=\tfrac{\text{area}}s$ for each half.
solution: The right angle is at $A$; $D$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so $AD=BD=DC=5$.
2017B21.shortcut: Recognise $6$-$8$-$10$ as right, and the median to the hypotenuse is $5$.
traps: Not noticing the right angle at $A$.
Using the whole triangle's area for each half.
2017B21.recognize: Medians in right triangles: the median to the hypotenuse equals half of it; medians split area equally.

2017B22.goal: $AB$ is a diameter of a circle of radius $2$; $D$ is $3$ beyond $B$ on line $AB$, and $E$ is $5$ above $D$. Line $AE$ meets the circle again at $C$. We want $[ABC]$. Since $AB$ is a diameter, $\angle ACB=90^\circ$.

tools.name: Thales
tools.why: An angle in a semicircle is right.

tools.name: Right-triangle trigonometry
tools.why: $\theta=\angle CAB=\angle EAD$.

2017B22.approach: Triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $C$ with hypotenuse $AB=4$, and its angle at $A$ equals the angle of line $AE$. Read that angle off the right triangle $ADE$, then $[ABC]=\tfrac12AC\cdot BC$.

steps.title: The angle at $A$
steps.explain: $AD=AB+BD=7$ and $DE=5$, so $AE=\sqrt{74}$, $\cos\theta=\tfrac7{\sqrt{74}}$, $\sin\theta=\tfrac5{\sqrt{74}}$.

check.q: If $AD=7$ and $DE=5$ with a right angle at $D$, what is $AE$?

steps.title: Legs of $ABC$
steps.explain: $AC=4\cos\theta=\tfrac{28}{\sqrt{74}}$, $BC=4\sin\theta=\tfrac{20}{\sqrt{74}}$.

check.q: In a right triangle with hypotenuse $4$ and $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, the adjacent leg is?

steps.title: Area
steps.explain: $[ABC]=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{28\cdot20}{74}=\tfrac{280}{74}=\tfrac{140}{37}$.

2017B22.bridge: Use the right angle at $C$ and the angle of $AE$ from triangle $ADE$.
2017B22.recognize: A chord from one end of a diameter: the triangle with the diameter is right-angled, and its shape is set by the chord's angle.

2017B23.goal: $N$ is the $79$-digit concatenation $123\ldots4344$. We want $N\bmod45$. Since $45=5\cdot9$, find $N$ mod $5$ and mod $9$ separately.

tools.name: Mod 5 from the last digit
tools.why: $10\equiv0\pmod5$.

tools.name: Mod 9 from the digit sum
tools.why: Each number's digit sum is congruent to the number mod $9$.

tools.name: Chinese remainder theorem
tools.why: $5$ and $9$ are coprime.

2017B23.approach: Mod $5$ is the last digit. For mod $9$, the digit sum of the concatenation is congruent to $1+2+\cdots+44$. Combine with CRT.

steps.title: Mod 5
steps.explain: $N$ ends in $4$, so $N\equiv4\pmod5$.

steps.title: Mod 9
steps.explain: $N\equiv1+2+\cdots+44=\tfrac{44\cdot45}{2}=990\equiv0\pmod9$.

steps.title: Combine
steps.explain: We need a multiple of $9$ that is $\equiv4\pmod5$: $0,9,18,27,36$ give $0,4,3,2,1$ mod $5$. So $N\equiv9\pmod{45}$.

2017B23.bridge: Get $N$ mod $5$ and mod $9$, then combine.
solution: The multiple of $9$ below $45$ that is $4\bmod5$ is $9$.
2017B23.shortcut: Concatenation mod $9$ equals the sum of the pieces mod $9$.
traps: Summing the actual digits instead of the numbers (works but slower).
2017B23.recognize: Large concatenated numbers mod a composite: split into coprime factors with easy tests (last digit, digit sum).

2017B24.goal: An equilateral triangle has its vertices on $xy=1$ and its centroid at the hyperbola's vertex $(1,1)$ (or $(-1,-1)$). We want the square of its area. For an equilateral triangle the centroid is also the circumcentre, so we need its circumradius.

tools.name: Centroid = circumcentre
tools.why: All medians are also perpendicular bisectors.

tools.name: Symmetry in $y=x$
tools.fact: \text{Circle centred on }y=x\text{ and }xy=1\text{ are both symmetric in }y=x
tools.why: So their (at most $4$) intersection points pair up across $y=x$ or lie on it; three vertices force one on $y=x$.

tools.name: Area from circumradius
tools.why: Three triangles from the centre, each $\tfrac12R^2\sin120^\circ$.

2017B24.approach: Take the centroid $(1,1)$. The circumcircle is centred at $(1,1)$; by symmetry in $y=x$, one vertex is on $y=x$, so it is $(-1,-1)$ (the point $(1,1)$ is the centre, not on the circle). Then $R^2=8$ and the area follows.

steps.title: Find a vertex
steps.explain: The circumcircle centred at $(1,1)$ and the hyperbola are both symmetric about $y=x$. Their intersection points come in mirror pairs or lie on $y=x$. Three vertices cannot all be in mirror pairs, so one lies on $y=x$ and on $xy=1$: that is $(-1,-1)$.

steps.title: Circumradius
steps.explain: $R$ is the distance from $(1,1)$ to $(-1,-1)$: $R^2=4+4=8$.

check.q: What is the squared distance from $(1,1)$ to $(-1,-1)$?

steps.title: Area squared
steps.explain: $[\triangle]=\tfrac{3\sqrt3}4\cdot8=6\sqrt3$, so its square is $108$.

2017B24.bridge: Use centroid = circumcentre, symmetry to place a vertex at $(-1,-1)$, and $[\triangle]=\tfrac{3\sqrt3}4R^2$.
solution: By symmetry in $y=x$, one vertex is $(-1,-1)$, so $R^2=8$.
traps: Placing a vertex at $(1,1)$ (that is the centre).
2017B24.recognize: Equilateral triangles with a known centre: centroid = circumcentre; symmetry of the setting often locates one vertex.

2017B25.goal: Isabella's $7$ distinct scores in $91$–$100$ have an integer average after every test, and the $7$th score is $95$. We want the $6$th. Integer averages mean divisibility of the running totals.

tools.name: Integer averages
tools.why: The average of the first $k$ scores is $S_k/k$.

tools.name: Bounding a sum
tools.why: Seven distinct integers in $[91,100]$.

2017B25.approach: $S_7$ is a multiple of $7$ between $658$ and $679$. $S_6=S_7-95$ must be a multiple of $6$. That pins $S_7$ and $S_6$. Then $S_5=S_6-a_6$ must be a multiple of $5$, restricting $a_6$.

steps.title: The sixth score
steps.explain: $S_5=570-a_6$ must be divisible by $5$, so $a_6\equiv0\pmod5$: $a_6\in\{95,100\}$. $95$ is the seventh score and scores are distinct, so $a_6=100$.

check.q: Which scores in $91$–$100$ are multiples of $5$?

2017B25.bridge: Use $7\mid S_7$, $6\mid S_6$, $5\mid S_5$ with the bounds.
solution: $S_7$ is a multiple of $7$ in $[658,679]$, and $S_7-95$ must be a multiple of $6$: only $S_7=665$, $S_6=570$.
2017B25.shortcut: Work backwards from the last test: each running total's divisibility shrinks the options quickly.
2017B25.recognize: "Every running average is an integer": the $k$-th total is divisible by $k$; combine with bounds and work backwards.
